title: The Garden That Grew Hope
summary: A neighborhood turns a trash-filled empty lot into a shared vegetable garden, and a shy girl discovers new friends and a love of growing things.
poll: Working together on a shared project is more rewarding than working alone.

versions.title: The Garden That Grew Hope
versions.text:
There was an empty lot on the street. It was full of trash and weeds. No one used it. Kids walked past it.

One day, old Mr. Nasser had a plan. He had a talk. "Let's make a garden," he said. The neighbors said yes.

They picked up trash. They pulled out weeds. Then they dug the dirt. Many hands helped.

A girl named Lina lived near. She was shy. She did not want to help. But her mom said, "Just try it."

Lina held a seed. She put it in dirt. She gave it water. Each day she came back.

Lina met a girl named Sara. They watered plants. They pulled weeds. Lina was not shy now. She had a new friend.

Plants grew big. Red fruit grew. Food grew under the dirt too. It was time for the harvest.

Neighbors picked the food. They gave it to every home. Lina smiled. She loved her garden.

At the end of a quiet street sat an empty lot. For years it was nothing but trash and tall, dry weeds, and nobody in the community ever bothered to use it. Children simply walked past it on their way to school.

One afternoon, an older neighbor named Mr. Nasser had an idea that would change the whole street. He gathered the community together for a short meeting. "Let's turn this empty lot into a garden," he suggested, and every neighbor who heard the plan quickly agreed to help.

Dozens of volunteers showed up that weekend. Together, they hauled away the old trash and pulled out the stubborn weeds. Then they dug up the hard, dry soil so that new plants would have room to grow. Cooperate as they did, the heavy work went much faster than anyone expected.

A quiet girl named Lina lived just down the street from the lot. She was shy, and at first she did not want to join the volunteers at all. Her mother gently encouraged her, saying, "Just try it once, and see how it feels."

Lina finally picked up a tiny seed and pressed it into the soft, dark soil. She watered her small plant with care every single day, and slowly, day after day, she returned just to check on its progress.

Soon Lina met another volunteer her own age named Sara. The two girls watered the young plants side by side and pulled stubborn weeds together as well. Lina was not shy anymore. Working in the garden had finally given her a true friend.

As the weeks passed, the plants began to flourish in the rich soil. Red fruit ripened on the leafy vines, while orange roots grew quietly beneath the surface. At last, the long-awaited harvest arrived.

Neighbors from every home gathered to pick the fresh vegetables together, laughing and chatting as they worked side by side. They shared full baskets of food with every family on the street. Lina smiled a wide, happy smile, because she had truly come to love gardening.

versions.title: The Garden That Grew Hope
versions.text:
At the end of a quiet residential street sat an empty, neglected lot that nobody particularly wanted, a forgotten patch of ground that had gradually accumulated trash and tall, desiccated weeds over several consecutive years. No one within the surrounding community ever demonstrated the initiative necessary to clean it up, even though it remained in plain sight every single day, and children simply walked past it on their way to school each morning without giving it a second glance.

One memorable afternoon, an older neighbor named Mr. Nasser conceived of an idea that would eventually transform the entire street in ways nobody could have accurately anticipated beforehand. He assembled the community for a brief, informal meeting outside his residence and proposed, "Let's convert this empty lot into a community garden where everyone can cultivate something meaningful together." Every neighbor who heard the proposal quickly consented to participate, since most of them had secretly wished the lot appeared more presentable for a considerable period already.

Dozens of enthusiastic volunteers arrived early the following weekend, prepared to collaborate extensively on the substantial labor awaiting them collectively. They hauled away the accumulated refuse, extracted the stubborn weeds, and excavated the hard, compacted soil so that new vegetation would finally possess adequate room to develop and spread its roots unimpeded. Because everyone chose to cooperate rather than struggle independently, the arduous labor proceeded far more rapidly than anyone had originally anticipated.

A reserved girl named Lina resided just down the street from the lot, and she noticed the sudden burst of activity immediately, observing curiously from behind her bedroom curtain. She was shy, however, and initially hesitated to join the volunteers, apprehensive that she would not understand what to do among so many unfamiliar faces. Her mother gently encouraged her, remarking, "Just attempt it once, and discover how it feels to contribute something genuinely meaningful."

Lina eventually retrieved a tiny seed and pressed it deliberately into the soft, dark soil adjacent to the fence, watering it with considerable care every single day without exception. Gradually, day after day, she returned simply to monitor its quiet progress, experiencing a small thrill whenever a new leaf unfurled itself toward the morning sunlight.

Soon Lina encountered another young volunteer named Sara, and the two girls rapidly became inseparable friends despite having never previously spoken before that particular weekend. They watered the developing plants side by side and extracted stubborn weeds together as well, conversing continuously about school, games, and the garden itself. Lina was no longer shy, because laboring in the garden had finally provided her with a genuine, enduring friendship.

As the weeks progressed, the plants began flourishing remarkably within the newly cultivated soil, growing considerably taller and stronger than anyone had originally anticipated. Red fruit ripened gradually upon the leafy vines, while orange roots developed quietly beneath the surface, concealed from view until harvest day ultimately arrived.

Neighbors representing every household congregated to harvest the fresh vegetables collectively, laughing and conversing as they labored side by side beneath the warm afternoon sunshine. Their generosity extended considerably beyond their own immediate families, since they transported full baskets of food to elderly neighbors who could no longer venture outside independently. Lina smiled a wide, contented smile, because she had genuinely come to cherish gardening with her entire heart, a passion she never could have anticipated discovering within herself.

It was full of trash and weeds
questions.why: The story says the lot was full of trash and weeds before anyone cleaned it.

wrong.A: There is no lake in the story.
wrong.B: The story does not mention snow.
wrong.C: The story does not mention a fence.

questions.stem: In the story, a seed is —
options: a tool used for digging up dirt
a small part that can grow into a plant
a kind of weed that grows wild
a basket used for carrying food
questions.why: The story says Lina put a seed in the soil, and it grew into a plant.

wrong.A: A seed is not a digging tool.
wrong.C: A weed is a different kind of plant.
wrong.D: A basket is not a seed.

questions.stem: Why did Lina not want to help at first?
options: She did not live close to the lot
She was shy
She was too busy with homework from school
She did not like plants or dirt
questions.why: The story says Lina was shy and did not want to help at first.

wrong.A: Lina lived close to the lot.
wrong.C: School is not mentioned as the reason.
wrong.D: The story never says she disliked plants.

questions.stem: Why did the author probably write this story?
options: To explain the steps for planting a tree
To describe a scary event that happens at night
To show how a messy lot and a shy girl can both change for the better
To teach readers how to drive a tractor safely
questions.why: The story shows the lot changing from trash to a garden, and Lina changing from shy to confident and happy.

wrong.A: The story does not give planting steps.
wrong.D: The story has nothing to do with tractors.

questions.stem: Why did Lina probably feel happy when she saw a new leaf grow?
options: She did not expect the seed to become a plant
She was proud of something she had helped grow
She was tired of waiting every day
She wanted to sell the new leaf
questions.why: Lina cared for the seed every day, so seeing it grow likely made her feel proud of her work.

wrong.A: She knew a seed grows into a plant.
wrong.C: Being tired of waiting would not explain her joy.
wrong.D: The story never mentions selling anything.

questions.stem: What can you tell about Lina by the end of the story?
options: She never spoke to Sara again after that day
She moved away from the street with her family
She still does not like the garden much
She made a friend and now loves gardening
questions.why: The story says Lina made a friend, Sara, and that she truly loved her garden by the end.

wrong.A: Lina and Sara worked together happily.
wrong.B: The story does not say Lina moved away.
wrong.C: The story says Lina loved the garden by the end.

LOW.prompt: Would you like to help start a garden like Lina did? Explain why or why not, using at least two facts from the story.
checklist: I clearly said what I think.
I used at least two facts from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: I would like to help start a garden like Lina did. I would want to plant a seed and watch it grow, just like she did with her small plant. I would also like to make a new friend while working, the way Lina made a friend named Sara. It sounds like hard work, but sharing the harvest with neighbors would feel nice.

questions.stem: What did the volunteers do before they could plant anything?
options: They painted the sidewalk near the lot
They hauled away trash and dug up the soil
They planted trees along the street first
They built a fence around the whole lot
questions.why: The story says the volunteers hauled away trash, pulled weeds, and dug up the soil before any plants could grow.

wrong.A: The story never mentions painting.
wrong.C: Trees are not planted in this story.
wrong.D: No fence is mentioned in the story.

questions.stem: What happened right after the vegetables were harvested?
options: The neighbors sold the vegetables at a market
Mr. Nasser kept all of the food for himself
The whole garden was quietly torn down
Neighbors shared the food with families on the street
questions.why: The story says that after the harvest, neighbors shared baskets of food with every family, including elderly neighbors.

wrong.A: No market or selling is described.
wrong.B: The food was shared with everyone, not kept by one person.
wrong.C: The garden is not torn down in the story.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?
options: A community works together to turn an empty lot into a garden, and a shy girl finds friendship along the way
A family argues loudly about who owns an old, empty lot
A group of scientists studies unusual plants inside a lab
Mr. Nasser quietly grows the whole garden by himself
questions.why: The story follows the whole community cleaning and planting the lot together, while Lina overcomes her shyness and gains a friend.

wrong.B: The neighbors agree right away; there is no argument.
wrong.C: No scientists or labs appear in the story.
wrong.D: Many volunteers help, not just Mr. Nasser.

questions.stem: In the story, the word cooperate means —
options: to sell something to another person for money
to work together with others
to hide quietly from other people
to compete hard against other people
questions.why: The story says the neighbors chose to cooperate, which let the work go faster, meaning they worked together.

wrong.A: No selling happens in the garden work.
wrong.C: Cooperating means joining in, not hiding.
wrong.D: The neighbors were helping, not competing.

questions.stem: Why did the heavy work go faster than expected?
options: A large machine dug up the entire lot
Only Mr. Nasser did all of the digging work
The neighbors cooperated instead of working alone
The stubborn weeds pulled themselves out
questions.why: The story says because everyone chose to cooperate, the heavy work went much faster than anyone expected.

wrong.A: No machine is mentioned in the story.
wrong.B: Dozens of volunteers helped, not just Mr. Nasser.

questions.stem: How does the author organize this story?
options: By comparing two completely different gardens side by side
By listing numbered steps for how to plant vegetables
By describing only one single day from morning to night
By describing the lot's problem, the community's solution, and Lina's change
questions.why: The story moves from the messy lot, to the community's cleanup and planting, to Lina's personal change and the final harvest.

wrong.A: Only one garden is described in the story.
wrong.B: The story is a narrative, not a numbered how-to list.
wrong.C: The story covers several weeks, not just one day.

questions.stem: Why did Lina's mother encourage her to try helping in the garden?
options: She needed Lina to stay home and watch the house
She wanted Lina to stop playing with her friend Sara
She hoped Lina would feel good about helping, even though she was shy
She wanted Lina to sell vegetables at a stand
questions.why: Lina's mother gently told her to just try it and see how it felt, suggesting she hoped Lina would benefit from joining in.

wrong.A: Watching the house is not mentioned.
wrong.B: Lina meets Sara later, in the garden.
wrong.D: No selling is mentioned by the mother.

questions.stem: How did working in the garden change how Lina felt about herself?
options: She stopped caring about her small plant entirely
She became shyer around people than she had been before
She decided gardening was too much work and quit
She became more confident and less shy after making a friend
questions.why: The story says that after meeting Sara and working together, Lina was not shy anymore and loved gardening.

wrong.A: She checked on her plant every day and cared deeply about it.
wrong.B: The story says she became less shy, not more.
wrong.C: The story shows Lina continuing happily, not quitting.

MID.prompt: Explain how both the neighborhood and Lina changed by the end of the story. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how the neighborhood changed.
I used at least two details from the story.
MID.modelAnswer: By the end of the story, both the neighborhood and Lina had changed. The empty lot, once full of trash and weeds, became a community garden full of ripe vegetables that neighbors shared with every family. Lina changed too: she started out shy and unwilling to help, but after planting a seed and meeting her new friend Sara, she became confident and discovered that she truly loved gardening.

keyWords.definition: a group of people who live in the same area
keyWords.example: The whole community came out to watch the parade.

keyWords.definition: the top layer of earth where plants grow
keyWords.example: Farmers check the soil before planting their crops.

keyWords.definition: a person who offers to help without being paid
keyWords.example: A volunteer handed out water bottles at the race.

keyWords.definition: to work together with other people toward the same goal
keyWords.example: The two teams had to cooperate to finish the project on time.

keyWords.definition: to grow very well and become healthy or successful
keyWords.example: The roses began to flourish once they got more sunlight.

questions.stem: What initiative did Mr. Nasser take at the beginning of the story?
options: He reported the empty lot to the city government
He hired outside workers to build houses on the lot
He proposed turning the lot into a community garden
He planted a whole garden secretly without telling anyone
questions.why: The story says Mr. Nasser gathered the community and proposed turning the lot into a garden where everyone could cultivate something together.

wrong.A: No government report is mentioned.
wrong.B: No houses are built in the story.
wrong.D: He openly gathered the whole community, rather than acting secretly.

questions.stem: In the story, the word generosity refers to —
options: a careful, detailed plan for growing vegetables
a willingness to give freely to others
a feeling of jealousy toward one's neighbors
a strict set of rules for using the garden
questions.why: The story describes the neighbors' generosity when they carry baskets of food to elderly neighbors who cannot come outside, showing a willingness to give.

wrong.A: The word describes an attitude, not a gardening plan.
wrong.C: The neighbors show kindness, not jealousy.
wrong.D: No strict rules are mentioned in the story.

questions.stem: In what order did these events happen?
options: The harvest is shared, and then Mr. Nasser has his idea
Lina meets Sara, and then Mr. Nasser has his idea
Volunteers clear the lot, and then the harvest is shared first
Mr. Nasser has his idea, volunteers clear the lot, Lina plants a seed
questions.why: Mr. Nasser's idea comes first, then volunteers clear and dig the lot, and only after that does Lina plant her seed.

wrong.A: The idea must come before the harvest, which happens much later.
wrong.B: Lina meets Sara only after the lot is cleared and she begins planting.
wrong.C: Clearing the lot comes well before the harvest is shared.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the story?
options: A single volunteer secretly repairs the lot overnight
The story argues that community gardens are too difficult to maintain
Mr. Nasser decides the garden is a failure and abandons it
A neglected lot and a reserved girl are both transformed through the community's effort
questions.why: The story links the community's collaborative transformation of the lot with Lina's personal transformation from shyness to confidence and generosity.

wrong.A: Dozens of volunteers work together; it is not done secretly by one person.
wrong.B: The garden succeeds, showing the opposite of this idea.
wrong.C: The garden flourishes and is never abandoned.

questions.stem: Based on the story, why were the elderly neighbors specifically given baskets of food?
options: Because they had already paid for the vegetables in advance
Because they personally had grown the most vegetables
Because they could not come outside to gather the harvest themselves
Because Mr. Nasser only liked certain neighbors on the street
questions.why: The story explains that neighbors carried food to elderly neighbors who could not come outside themselves, showing thoughtful generosity.

wrong.A: No payment is mentioned in the story.
wrong.B: The story does not rank neighbors by how much they grew.
wrong.D: The story shows generosity to the whole community, not favoritism.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe Lina hesitating before joining the volunteers?
options: To suggest that Lina disliked gardening from the very start
To show that overcoming shyness is part of her transformation across the story
To show that the other volunteers rejected her at first
To explain why the garden eventually failed to grow
questions.why: Lina's early hesitation sets up her later growth, when she becomes confident and makes a true friend through the garden.

wrong.A: By the end, Lina loves gardening deeply.
wrong.C: No volunteer rejects Lina in the story.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the detail that Lina and Sara had never spoken before that weekend?
options: To suggest that Sara was new to the entire neighborhood
To show that the two girls disliked each other at first
To explain why the garden's plants grew so quickly
To emphasize that the shared garden project created their friendship
questions.why: Highlighting that the girls were strangers before working together underscores how collaborating on the garden, not prior acquaintance, built their friendship.

wrong.A: The story never says Sara was new to the area.
wrong.B: The girls become close quickly, with no sign of dislike.
wrong.C: Their friendship does not explain the plants' growth.

questions.stem: What can readers infer from the fact that Lina returned to check on her seed every single day?
options: She distrusted the advice her mother had given her
She was worried that someone would steal the seed
She wanted to replace the seed with a different one
She was developing real care and interest in gardening
questions.why: Daily, attentive visits to a growing plant suggest genuine investment and growing interest, which matches her later love of gardening.

wrong.A: Her mother's advice is what led her to try gardening in the first place.
wrong.B: No theft or danger to the seed is mentioned.
wrong.C: The story never suggests she wanted a different seed.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says working together is more rewarding than working alone. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story about the garden project and Lina's experience.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that working together is more rewarding than working alone. The volunteers finished the heavy work on the lot far faster because they cooperated instead of struggling individually, and the shared harvest let the whole street benefit, including elderly neighbors who could not help themselves. Lina's experience shows this too: by joining the group effort instead of staying home alone, she gained both a new skill and a true friend in Sara. Someone might argue that working alone lets a person move at their own pace without waiting for others, but the garden's quick transformation and Lina's new friendship show how much more can be gained by joining with others.

keyWords.definition: to work jointly with others on a shared task
keyWords.example: The two scientists collaborated on a new experiment.

keyWords.definition: to prepare land and grow plants on it
keyWords.example: Her grandparents cultivate a small field of wheat every year.

keyWords.definition: to change something completely, often for the better
keyWords.example: New paint and lights can transform a dull room.

keyWords.definition: the ability to decide and act on something without being told to
keyWords.example: He showed initiative by organizing the cleanup himself.

keyWords.definition: the quality of being willing to give freely to others
keyWords.example: Her generosity was clear when she shared her lunch with a new student.
